questions.prompt: Which type of app launch is the slowest because iOS must create a new process and load the app from disk?

options.explanation: Right. In a cold launch, the app is not in memory or system cache, so iOS starts from scratch.
In a warm launch, parts of the binary are already cached in memory, making it faster.
During a resume, the app is already suspended in memory, so no new process starts.
Prewarming loads libraries before the user taps, so it is faster than a full cold launch.

questions.prompt: What happens when iOS resumes a suspended app from the background?

options.text: The dynamic linker reloads all dynamic libraries from disk.
options.explanation: Dynamic libraries stay loaded when the app is suspended in memory.

options.text: The app moves back to the foreground without creating a new process.
options.explanation: Right. A suspended app is already in memory, so iOS wakes it without starting a new process.

options.text: The system deletes all cached view controllers and restarts from main.
options.explanation: Resuming keeps the existing process and views unless the OS terminated the app.

options.text: Xcode runs all static initializers again before showing the screen.
options.explanation: Static initializers run during a fresh process launch, not on resume.

questions.prompt: What does `dyld` do during the pre-main phase of a cold launch?

options.text: It draws the first SwiftUI view on the GPU.
options.explanation: UI rendering happens after main starts, during the post-main phase.

options.text: It connects the first UIScene to the window.
options.explanation: Scene connection happens post-main inside UIKit lifecycle callbacks.

options.text: It loads the app binary and dynamic libraries, then fixes memory addresses.
options.explanation: Right. The dynamic linker maps libraries, resolves symbols, and runs static initializers before main.

options.text: It downloads remote configuration files from the backend.
options.explanation: Network requests are app code that runs after main, not dyld work.

questions.prompt: Which kind of code runs automatically before `main` during app launch and slows down pre-main time?

options.explanation: Swift static properties initialize lazily on first access, not before main.
View lifecycle methods run after main, once views appear.
SwiftUI modifiers run during the post-main view lifecycle.

options.text: Objective-C `+load` methods and C++ static constructors
options.explanation: Right. Static initializers like +load and C++ static constructors execute before main starts.

questions.prompt: What milestone marks the end of the initial visible startup for a user?

options.text: The app draws its first frame on screen.
options.explanation: Right. Users judge launch speed by how fast the first frame appears on screen.

options.text: The app finishes uploading analytics events.
options.explanation: Analytics should run after the first frame, not before it.

options.text: The compiler finishes building the binary in Xcode.
options.explanation: Build time happens on the developer machine, not when the user opens the app.

options.text: The user puts the app into the background.
options.explanation: Backgrounding happens when the user leaves the app, not when it starts.

questions.prompt: How do Xcode mergeable libraries help both developer build speed and cold launch time?

options.text: They skip compiling framework code during Debug builds.
options.explanation: Xcode still compiles framework targets in Debug builds.

options.text: They convert Objective-C frameworks into Swift macros automatically.
options.explanation: Mergeable libraries control linking, not language conversion.

options.text: They link frameworks dynamically even inside App Store Release builds.
options.explanation: Keeping frameworks dynamic in Release builds would hurt launch time.

options.text: They stay dynamic in Debug for fast builds and merge into the binary in Release.
options.explanation: Right. Merging in Release builds removes dyld dynamic library overhead while keeping Debug builds fast.

questions.prompt: In 2–5 sentences, explain the difference between a cold launch, a warm launch, and a resume.

rubric.criterion: Explains cold launch: app is not in memory or cache, so OS starts a new process and loads everything
Explains warm launch: process is not running, but parts of the binary stay cached in memory
Explains resume: app is already suspended in memory and returns without a new process launch

questions.modelAnswer: A cold launch happens when the app is not in memory or system cache, so iOS creates a new process and loads everything from disk. A warm launch happens when the process ended, but parts of the binary remain cached in memory. A resume happens when the app is already suspended in memory, so iOS brings it back without starting a new process.

questions.prompt: In 2–5 sentences, explain what happens during the pre-main phase and list two ways to make it faster.

rubric.criterion: States that dyld loads the binary and dynamic libraries and static initializers run before main
Gives first valid speedup (reducing dynamic frameworks or using mergeable libraries)
Gives second valid speedup (removing Objective-C +load or C++ static constructors)

questions.modelAnswer: During the pre-main phase, dyld loads the app binary and dynamic libraries, fixes memory addresses, and runs static initializers. To make pre-main faster, reduce the number of dynamic frameworks or merge them in Release builds using mergeable libraries. You should also remove static initializers such as Objective-C +load methods and C++ static constructors.

questions.prompt: In 2–5 sentences, explain why you should measure launch time on a real device in Release mode instead of Debug on the Simulator. Name the Xcode tool you use.

rubric.criterion: States that Debug builds turn off optimizations and add extra runtime checks
States that the Simulator uses faster Mac hardware instead of real iPhone CPU and storage
Mentions profiling on a real device in Release configuration with Instruments

questions.modelAnswer: Debug builds turn off compiler optimizations and add extra checks, which makes startup look slower in some places. At the same time, the Simulator runs on a fast Mac CPU and SSD, which hides real iPhone delays. To get real numbers, always profile a Release build on a real device using the App Launch template in Instruments.

questions.prompt: In 2–5 sentences, explain what app prewarming is and what bug it can cause with Keychain reads after a reboot. Say how to avoid that bug.

rubric.criterion: Defines prewarming: iOS starts the process and loads libraries early, then pauses it before user opens it
Explains the bug: early launch after a reboot can happen before the user unlocks the phone, so protected storage is unavailable
States the fix: delay reading user secrets until the scene is active or protected data is unlocked

questions.modelAnswer: App prewarming means iOS starts your app process early, loads linked libraries, and pauses it before user code runs. After a device reboot, early launch work can happen before the user unlocks the phone. If your code reads Keychain secrets or protected files right away, those reads can fail, so check isProtectedDataAvailable and wait until the scene becomes active.

questions.prompt: In 2–5 sentences, describe how you measure launch time locally, in automated tests, and in production.

rubric.criterion: Locally: Instruments App Launch template and OSSignposter intervals on a real device
Automated tests: XCTApplicationLaunchMetric in XCTest UI tests
Production: Xcode Organizer and MetricKit launch histograms (TimeToFirstDrawMetric via MetricResult, or older MXAppLaunchMetric)

questions.modelAnswer: Locally, I profile a Release build on a real device with the App Launch template in Instruments and use OSSignposter intervals for custom startup steps. In automated CI tests, I add XCTApplicationLaunchMetric to catch regressions before merging code. In production, I track real user launch histograms in Xcode Organizer and MetricKit using TimeToFirstDrawMetric inside MetricResult (or MXAppLaunchMetric in older OS versions).
